Case Vignette: "Saoirse"

Saoirse is a 57-year-old married woman of South Eastern Asian descent who presents for therapy at the urging of her husband. She is a midwife, a role she has held for over thirty years. She speaks in a low, measured tone, her hands folded tightly in her lap, and she often pauses to look at the floor before answering a question.

The event that shattered her world happened twenty-two years ago, when she was 35. She had just finished a night shift at the hospital, a long and complicated delivery that had ended with a healthy baby and a grateful mother. She was walking to her car in the hospital parking garage, a route she had taken hundreds of times. A man, a stranger, came up from behind her. He had a knife. He forced her into the back of her own car. He raped her. He told her if she screamed, he would kill her. He said he knew where she lived. He left her there, in the back seat, bleeding and shaking, as the sun began to rise.

Saoirse did not call the police. She did not tell her husband. She drove home, took a shower so hot it scalded her skin, and went to work the next day. She told herself it was over. She told herself she was fine. She was a midwife. She brought life into the world. She could not be broken.

For the first few years, she managed. She threw herself into her work, taking extra shifts, volunteering for the most difficult cases. She found a strange, grim comfort in the controlled chaos of the delivery room. But the nightmares started. Not every night, but often enough. In the dream, she is always in the parking garage. The fluorescent lights are too bright. The concrete walls are too close. She can smell the exhaust and the antiseptic. She can feel the cold metal of the knife against her throat. She wakes up gasping, her heart hammering, her sheets soaked with sweat.

She began to avoid certain things. She stopped working night shifts. She asked for a parking spot near the entrance. She always walked to her car with her keys clutched between her fingers like a weapon. She stopped going to the grocery store after dark. She stopped going to the movies. She stopped having sex with her husband. She would find reasons-a headache, exhaustion, a demanding patient. The truth was that the thought of being touched, of being vulnerable, sent a jolt of pure terror through her body. She could feel his hands on her skin, his breath on her neck.

Her husband, a kind and patient man, grew confused and then resentful. He thought he had done something wrong. He thought she didn't love him anymore. Saoirse could not explain it to him. She could not find the words. The shame was a physical weight in her chest. She felt dirty. She felt like a fraud. She was the one who held the hands of laboring women, who whispered encouragement, who helped them feel safe. But she herself had never felt safe again.

In the delivery room, she has become hypervigilant. She notices everything. The angle of the lights. The position of the door. The tone of a doctor's voice. She can read a room full of people in seconds. She knows who is anxious, who is angry, who is a potential threat. This skill helps her in her work, but it is exhausting. She cannot turn it off. She carries a constant, low-grade dread, like a hum in her bones.

She is here now because she nearly collapsed last week. A patient was brought in from a car accident, a young woman covered in blood, screaming. The sound of her screams, the smell of the blood, the bright overhead lights-it all collapsed into one overwhelming moment. Saoirse froze. She couldn't move. She couldn't breathe. She saw the parking garage. She saw the knife. She saw the man's face. A colleague had to pull her away. She went into the bathroom and vomited.

Now, sitting in the quiet of the therapy room, she looks older than 57. She is a woman who has been holding a terrible secret for over two decades. She speaks about her work with love and pride, but her voice cracks when she describes the parking garage. She does not know if she can ever be free of it. She does not know if she deserves to be.
